name: How the FDA Itself Uses AI
blurb: Elsa and the FDA's consolidated data platform.
title: How the FDA Itself Uses AI
answer: The FDA now uses generative AI in its own reviews. Its Elsa tool helps staff search and summarise submissions, and in May 2026 the agency said it had consolidated more than 40 submission data systems into one platform with expanded AI capabilities, while keeping subject matter experts responsible for verifying inputs and conclusions.

reading.body:
The FDA now uses generative AI in its own reviews, with Elsa helping staff search and summarise submissions and human experts verifying every input and conclusion.

The pattern is consolidation before capability. More than 40 submission data systems were merged into one platform in May 2026, and the expanded AI capabilities arrived on top of that merged base. Generative search and summarisation work on a corpus that has already been unified, which is why the agency could add them at all. The compute and storage layer came first, and the model came second.

For life sciences teams this shifts the review, not the standard. Inconsistencies between documents become easier for the agency to find, so submissions that once passed on volume now face faster cross checking. The FDA states that subject matter experts remain responsible for verifying inputs and conclusions, so the accountability chain is unchanged even as the search gets faster.

What this does not cover is scale. The data gives no model, no vendor, no volume of submissions processed, and no error rate. It also says nothing about the compute or power behind the platform, so the infrastructure story here is a consolidation count rather than a capacity figure.

explainer:
The FDA has become a user of AI as well as a regulator of it. Its generative AI assistant, Elsa, was introduced to help reviewers and investigators read and summarise documents, compare information across submissions and speed routine tasks. In 2026 the agency described consolidating dozens of separate submission data systems into a single platform with expanded AI capabilities, while stating that its experts remain responsible for verifying inputs and conclusions.

For sponsors the practical effect is that the agency can search, cross reference and check submissions faster than before. Inconsistencies between modules, between a submission and earlier correspondence, or between stated and tabulated results are easier to find. It also signals that the agency is comfortable with AI in regulated work when people stay accountable, the same standard it applies to industry.

developments.text: The FDA announced expanded AI capabilities and the completion of its data platform consolidation, with human verification at every stage.
